newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Kohl seeks entrepreneurial culture shift.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kohl seeks entrepreneurial culture shift.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday told Germans they needed to be more entrepreneurial and urged young people not immediately to seek the easy option of working within a large organisation.
Speaking at a Frankfurt conference for German small and medium companies, the famous "Mittelstand", Kohl said "a new culture" was needed in which self-employed and entrepreneurs could flourish.
"The finance sector in particular must be more courageous and ready to take risks in launching young people with good ideas into self-employment," he said.

Kohl, who has in the past accused Germans of basking in a "collective leisure park", said it was "understandable" that young people still preferred the shorter hours and job security offered by large, often state-run organisations.
"But we have to consider whether this is still possible," he said.

He added that an economy where state salaries made up half of total earnings could no longer operate, insisting that public spending should fall below the pre-unification figure of 46 percent of gross domestic product from its current level of over 50 percent.

Kohl was speaking amid increasing conflict between trade unions and employers over new government measures aimed at cutting Germany's generous sick pay system, one of main benefits available to German employees.

He was earlier on Tuesday labelled a "political pharisee" by the head of the powerful IG Metall trade union for his role in pushing through new austerity measures that will result in cuts to a sick pay system that currently offers full salary even for long-term sickness.

But Kohl insisted in his speech that the austerity package had to be completed and quoted a report by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Decelopment (OECD) suggesting that further measures might even be necessary.

"I couldn't have put it better myself," he said. The German government is aiming to slash some 70 billion marks from government spending next year to help it qualify for Europe's planned single currency.
